terms.definition: One version of a gene; different alleles create different traits, like different flower colors.
terms.function: Occupies a locus on a chromosome and, together with its paired allele, determines the genotype for that gene.
terms.whereItIs: Seated at a specific locus on a chromosome, inside the nucleus of nearly every cell.
terms.whyItMatters: Alleles are the reason offspring resemble both parents but are never an exact copy of either one.

terms.definition: A segment of DNA that carries instructions for one trait; a gene is like a question, and its alleles are the possible answers.
terms.function: Defines which trait a locus controls; the specific instruction actually carried there is determined by which allele is present.
terms.whereItIs: A defined location (locus) on a chromosome.
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding that a gene is the category and an allele is one version of it is the key distinction this whole component teaches.

terms.definition: The specific location on a chromosome where a particular gene (and its alleles) is found.
terms.function: Marks the shared physical position on both chromosome copies where the two paired alleles for a gene are seated.
terms.whereItIs: A fixed point along a chromosome's length, shown as a thin ring around the chromosome rod in this model.
terms.whyItMatters: Both alleles for a gene must be at the same locus on their matching chromosomes for them to pair up and be compared.

terms.definition: An allele whose trait appears in the body even if only one copy of it is present.
terms.function: Masks the recessive allele's trait in the phenotype whenever the two are paired together (heterozygous).
terms.whereItIs: Written with a capital letter (e.g. P); shown as the bold terracotta token in the model.
terms.whyItMatters: Dominant alleles are why a trait can appear in a child even if only one parent visibly carries it.

terms.definition: An allele whose trait only appears in the body when both inherited copies are recessive.
terms.function: Its trait is masked in the phenotype whenever paired with a dominant allele, but it's still carried and can be passed to offspring.
terms.whereItIs: Written with a lowercase letter (e.g. p); shown as the muted, outlined sand token in the model.
terms.whyItMatters: Recessive alleles explain how a trait can 'skip a generation' — two parents who don't show it can still both carry and pass it on.

terms.definition: Having two identical alleles for a gene (both dominant, like PP, or both recessive, like pp).
terms.function: When homozygous recessive (pp), there's no dominant allele present to mask the trait, so the recessive phenotype is visible.
terms.whereItIs: Shown in the model when both locus tokens match — both bold-terracotta or both muted-sand.
terms.whyItMatters: Homozygous recessive is the only pairing where a recessive trait actually becomes visible.

terms.definition: Having two different alleles for a gene (one dominant, one recessive, like Pp).
terms.function: The dominant allele's trait shows in the phenotype while the recessive allele is masked but still carried.
terms.whereItIs: The model's default state — one bold-terracotta token opposite one muted-sand token.
terms.whyItMatters: Most 'carriers' of a recessive trait are heterozygous — they show the dominant trait but can still pass the recessive allele to their children.

terms.definition: The specific pair of alleles an organism has for a gene (e.g., Pp).
terms.function: Determines the phenotype according to the dominant/recessive relationship between the two alleles present.
terms.whereItIs: Read directly off the two locus tokens in the model — e.g. one dominant + one recessive token reads as 'Pp.'
terms.whyItMatters: Genotype is the underlying 'code'; phenotype is what you actually see — the two can differ, which is the whole point of recessive alleles.

terms.definition: The physical trait that actually shows up because of the genotype (e.g., purple flowers).
terms.function: The observable outcome produced once the dominant/recessive relationship between the two alleles in the genotype is resolved.
terms.whereItIs: The visible trait a genotype produces — not shown directly on the model itself, but the result the side panel reports for each pairing state.
terms.whyItMatters: Phenotype is what natural selection, breeders, and doctors can actually observe — genotype is what's inherited and passed on.
